displayQuote: A moral system valid for all is basically immoral

meta.title: Who really said "A moral system valid for all is basically immoral"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Nietzsche’s own words — it’s biographer Curtis Cate’s 2002 paraphrase of Beyond Good and Evil §221. The idea is Nietzsche’s; the exact wording isn’t.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A moral system valid for all is basically immoral'?
meta.ogDescription: The polished epigram is biographer Curtis Cate’s 2002 compression of Nietzsche’s Beyond Good and Evil §221 — a real Nietzschean idea in someone else’s words.

answer.label: Not Friedrich Nietzsche — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Nietzsche’s — it compresses aphorism 221 of ‘Beyond Good and Evil’ (1886), where he calls it “immoral” to insist that “what is right for one is proper for another.” But this exact, quotable sentence is not his: Wikiquote traces it to biographer Curtis Cate’s ‘Friedrich Nietzsche’ (2002), where it appears as Cate’s own paraphrase of §221.

source.heading: Where the words actually come from
source.excerpt: Moral systems must be compelled first of all to bow before the gradations of rank… until they thoroughly understand at last that it is immoral to say that ‘what is right for one is proper for another.’
trail: The line is filed under Misattributed on Wikiquote’s Beyond Good and Evil page, which states it is “a quotation from Curtis Cate’s Friedrich Nietzsche: A Biography (2003)… the author’s interpretation of Nietzsche’s Aphorism 221.”
The genuine §221 — readable in Zimmern’s public-domain translation at American Literature — makes the same point with different words.
Quote sites such as Goodreads circulate the epigram under Nietzsche’s name with no book, chapter, or page — the classic signature of a repackaged paraphrase.
source.excerptNote: This is the genuine passage from §221 (Zimmern’s 1907 translation). The familiar one-liner — “A moral system valid for all is basically immoral” — is Curtis Cate’s compression of the idea, not a sentence Nietzsche wrote.
source.rightsHolder: Estate of Curtis Cate and his publishers (Hutchinson, London; The Overlook Press, US)
source.rightsNote: The idea traces to Nietzsche’s ‘Beyond Good and Evil’ (1886), long in the public domain. But this page’s exact wording originates in Curtis Cate’s biography ‘Friedrich Nietzsche’ (Hutchinson, 2002; Overlook, 2005), which is well within copyright, so the sentence as quoted is in-copyright.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: Whose thought this really is
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German philosopher whose critiques of morality, truth, and religion reshaped modern thought. In ‘Beyond Good and Evil’ (1886) he attacked the idea of a single morality binding on everyone — the very argument this epigram condenses. He is also one of the internet’s most quote-magnetized names, so lines ‘about’ his ideas are routinely repackaged as things he literally wrote.

cite.sourceCitation: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, §221 (1886), trans. Helen Zimmern (New York: Macmillan, 1907). The popular epigram derives from Curtis Cate, Friedrich Nietzsche: A Biography (London: Hutchinson, 2002; Woodstock, NY: The Overlook Press, 2005).

misattribution.heading: The misattribution, untangled
misattribution.intro: This is a subtle case: not a fabrication and not a wrong author, but a biographer’s summary sentence that got promoted into a direct Nietzsche quotation.

items.why: The sentence “A moral system valid for all is basically immoral” is not found in Nietzsche’s writings. Wikiquote documents it as a line from Curtis Cate’s biography — the biographer’s interpretation of aphorism 221, later quoted as if Nietzsche said it.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is authentically Nietzsche’s (Beyond Good and Evil §221), but the crisp wording belongs to his biographer Curtis Cate (2002) — so quote it as a paraphrase, not a direct quotation.

context.heading: Why the idea matters
lead: In §221 of ‘Beyond Good and Evil,’ Nietzsche argues that any “unegoistic” morality that declares itself unconditional and binding on everyone is not just tasteless but harmful — a leveling force that injures “the higher, rarer” types. He drives the point to a deliberate provocation: it is, he says, immoral to insist that what is right for one is right for all.
Cate’s one-line distillation captures that provocation neatly — which is exactly why it travels so well and gets mistaken for Nietzsche’s own aphorism.
context.pull: The idea is Nietzsche’s; the sentence is his biographer’s.
